stem: Complete the code so that `backup` is a separate copy of `scores`, and the program prints `3 4`.
code:
scores = [70, 85, 90]
backup = scores__BLANK1__
backup.append(100)
print(len(scores), len(backup))

blanks.rationale: A full slice such as `[:]` builds a new list with the same items, so appending to the copy leaves the original alone.

explanation: `backup = scores` alone would make both names refer to the same list, and the program would print 4 4. Slicing the whole list with `scores[:]` creates a new list, so only `backup` grows.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.rationale: This counts positions from 1 instead of 0: index 1 is 10, the second item.
The first slice takes indexes 1, 3 and 5. The second starts at the last item and jumps back three places at a time: indexes 6, 3 and 0.
Index 5 is still below the stop value 6, so 30 is included.
A negative step walks backwards, so the slice starts with the last item, 35.

explanation: numbers[1:6:2] starts at index 1 (10), jumps by 2 to index 3 (20) and index 5 (30), and stops before index 6. numbers[::-3] has no start or stop, and its step is negative, so it starts at the last item (35, index 6) and moves back three places each time: index 3 (20), then index 0 (5).

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
empty = []
mixed = [3, "three", 3.0, True, []]
print(len(empty), len(mixed), mixed[-1])

options.rationale: [] holds no items at all, so its length is 0.
The empty list inside mixed is an item too, so it counts and it is the last one.

options.text: An error is raised, because a list can't mix types
options.rationale: A list may hold values of any types at the same time, including another list.
The empty list has no items, mixed has five items of different types, and its last item is an empty list.

explanation: len() counts the items in a list. empty has none, so len(empty) is 0. mixed holds an int, a string, a float, a bool and an empty list: five items. Mixing types in one list is allowed. The index -1 picks the last item, which is the empty list [].

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
fruits = ["fig", "kiwi"]
basket = fruits
spare = fruits[:]
basket.append("lime")
spare[0] = "date"
print(fruits)
print(spare)

options.rationale: basket is another name for the same list as fruits, while spare is a separate copy.
basket = fruits does not copy anything, so appending to basket changes fruits as well.
fruits[:] builds a new list, so changes to spare do not reach fruits, and the append to basket does not reach spare.
spare was copied before the append, and it is a separate list, so it never gets "lime".

explanation: basket = fruits gives the same list a second name, so basket.append("lime") changes the list that fruits also refers to. spare = fruits[:] makes a new list with copies of the items as they were at that moment. Changing spare[0] only changes the copy.

stem: Which line, inserted at the marked spot, makes the program print `[9, 7, 5, 3, 1]`?

options.rationale: The stop index 0 is not included, so the 1 at the front is left out.
A step of 1 goes forwards, so this is an unchanged copy.
With a negative step, the start must be to the right of the stop; here it is not, so the slice is empty.
A step of -1 with no start or stop walks through the whole list from the back.

explanation: [::-1] is the short way to get a reversed copy of a list: leaving out start and stop means "the whole list", and the step -1 walks it from the last item to the first.

stem: Which of the following expressions create a list holding values of different data types? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Square brackets create a list, and its items may be an integer, a string and a float.
A list can even contain another list and `None` next to a string.
Round brackets create a tuple, not a list.
`list()` accepts a single iterable, so three arguments raise a `TypeError`.
Quotes make this one string; it holds no separate items.

explanation: A list literal uses square brackets with items separated by commas, and the items need not share a type. Round brackets build a tuple, and `list()` takes one iterable rather than a series of values.
